---
title: "climatekit: Unified Climate Indices for Temperature, Precipitation, and Drought in R"
author:
  - name: Charles Coverdale
    affiliation: "London, United Kingdom"
    address: "United Kingdom"

    url: https://github.com/charlescoverdale/climatekit
abstract: >
  The \CRANpkg{climatekit} package computes the standard suite of
  climate indices from daily weather observations in a single R
  interface. Thirty functions cover temperature (frost days, ice
  days, summer days, growing and heating degree days, tropical
  nights, diurnal range, growing-season length, warm-spell duration),
  precipitation (wet and dry spells, heavy-precipitation days,
  one-day and five-day maxima, precipitation intensity), drought
  (Standardised Precipitation Index, Standardised
  Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index, potential evapotranspiration
  via the Hargreaves method), agroclimatology (Huglin, Winkler,
  Branas, frost dates), and thermal comfort (wind chill, heat index,
  humidex, fire danger). Definitions follow the Expert Team on
  Sector-specific Climate Indices recommendations
  (Zhang et al. 2011) where applicable. Every function returns a
  tidy data frame with a period, a value, an index name, and a unit,
  so outputs compose directly. The package is pure computation, has
  no API calls, and is available on CRAN.
preamble: |

## Introduction

The \CRANpkg{climatekit} package consolidates thirty climate indices
behind a single consistent interface. Each function takes daily
vectors (temperature, precipitation, humidity) with an accompanying
date vector and returns a data frame with four columns: \code{period}
(the reporting period, typically annual or monthly), \code{value}
(the index value), \code{index} (a character name), and \code{unit}.
Users can feed any output directly into plotting, tabulation, or
further aggregation without reshaping.

Climate-index analysis is a routine operation across applied climate
work: national meteorological services publish annual index tables,
regional climate assessments benchmark stations against one another,
agricultural and viticultural research tracks growing-season
indices, insurance underwriters use drought indices in parametric
products, and public-health authorities monitor heat-index exceedances.
Until now, the R ecosystem has exposed parts of this analysis
piecemeal, with separate packages for drought indices
(\CRANpkg{SPEI}), for standard climate-change indices
(\pkg{climdex.pcic}, archived), and for various agricultural indices.
\CRANpkg{climatekit} unifies the set.

The package has no network access, no external data dependency, and
no runtime requirements beyond \CRANpkg{cli} and base R. Users pair
it with a data-acquisition package (\CRANpkg{readnoaa} for NOAA's
Global Historical Climatology Network, \CRANpkg{rnoaa} for broader
NOAA holdings, or direct downloads from a national met service)
and pass the resulting daily series straight in.

## Background

Climate-index standardisation dates to @frich2002observed, who
proposed twenty-seven indices targeted at climate-change detection,
and continued through the joint CCl/WCRP/JCOMM Expert Team on
Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI), now the Expert Team
on Sector-specific Climate Indices (ET-SCI). @zhang2011indices
synthesised the ET-SCI core set, which informs most modern national
climate assessments. Applied analyses of the ETCCDI indices on
observed station records [@alexander2006global] and on gridded
reconstructions [@donat2013hadex2] document robust multi-decadal
trends. @sillmann2013indices evaluate the same indices across CMIP5
climate-model output, establishing the index suite as the bridge
between observational and model-based climate-change attribution.

**Temperature indices.** The core definitions are threshold counts
(frost days where $T_{\min} < 0^\circ$C; tropical nights where
$T_{\min} \geq 20$; summer days where $T_{\max} \geq 25$; ice days
where $T_{\max} < 0$) and degree-day accumulations (growing degree
days above a base, heating degree days below a reference, cooling
degree days above a reference). Diurnal range, growing-season
length, and warm-spell duration round out the temperature family.

**Precipitation indices.** Consecutive dry and wet days summarise
spell length. Total accumulation, heavy-precipitation exceedances,
and one- and five-day maxima summarise intensity. The simple daily
intensity index (SDII) is the average daily total on wet days. The
ETCCDI-standard thresholds for heavy-precipitation counts are the
95th (R95p) and 99th (R99p) percentiles of the wet-day
distribution at each station; \code{ck\_heavy\_precip()} accepts
an explicit \code{threshold} argument so users can supply either a
fixed value or a station-specific percentile computed from the
data.

**Drought indices.** @mckee1993relationship introduced the
Standardised Precipitation Index (SPI), which fits a gamma
distribution to precipitation accumulated over a chosen window
(three, six, twelve months) and standardises to a standard normal.
Values below minus one indicate moderate drought; below minus
two, extreme drought. @vicente2010multiscalar extended this to the
Standardised Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), which
incorporates potential evapotranspiration via a climatic water
balance. @stagge2015candidate compare candidate distributions for
both indices and find that the gamma family (for SPI) and the
generalised logistic (for SPEI) perform best in terms of
normality-of-residuals tests; \CRANpkg{climatekit} uses these
defaults. Potential evapotranspiration is computed by the
@hargreaves1985reference method from temperature extremes and
extra-terrestrial radiation.

**Agroclimatic indices.** The Huglin heliothermal index
[@huglin1978nouveau] accumulates heat summed between a base
temperature and a latitude-adjusted day length; it is the primary
viticultural suitability index in temperate Europe.
@tonietto2004multicriteria propose a multicriteria climatic
classification that combines the Huglin index with cool-night and
dryness indices, and supply the classification bands (HI-3 for cool
varieties, HI-2 for temperate, HI-1 for warm, plus subdivisions)
used in viticultural planning. The Winkler index
[@winkler1974general] is a similar cumulative heat metric used
widely in California. Branas, Bernon, and Levadoux's index is the
French viticultural analogue. First-frost and last-frost dates set
the frost-free growing window.

**Thermal comfort.** The US National Weather Service's heat index
[@rothfusz1990heat] converts temperature and humidity into an
apparent-temperature equivalent; Canadian humidex
[@masterton1979humidex] does the same with a different functional
form. Wind chill [@osczevski2005new] is the cold-weather counterpart.
Fire-weather indices combine temperature, humidity, wind, and
precipitation history.

## Package design

### Architecture

\CRANpkg{climatekit} is pure R with no compiled code. Runtime
imports are \CRANpkg{cli}, \code{stats}, and \code{tools}. R 4.1.0
or later is required. The test suite contains over a hundred tests
covering every exported function and every index definition.

### Uniform output format

Every index function returns a data frame with four columns:
\code{period}, \code{value}, \code{index}, and \code{unit}. The
\code{period} is a \code{Date} keyed to the start of the reporting
window (year or month); the \code{value} is numeric; \code{index}
and \code{unit} are character strings. This invariant means output
from any function composes directly into a larger panel via
\code{rbind()}, and plotting code is shared across index families.

### Uniform input signature

Every index function takes one or two daily numeric vectors plus a
\code{dates} vector of matching length. Where appropriate, a
\code{period} argument selects annual or monthly aggregation. Users
do not pass data frames; users pass the three or four vectors they
have.

### Generic dispatcher and metadata

\code{ck\_compute()} dispatches to any index by name, letting users
select the index programmatically from a configuration file or
argument. \code{ck\_available()} lists the indices that can be
computed given a supplied set of inputs; \code{ck\_metadata()}
returns each index's definition, unit, reference, and typical use.

### Reproducibility

Numerical results are deterministic given the input. The SPI and
SPEI implementations use gamma-distribution fitting, which is
deterministic up to the solver's numerical tolerance. All index
definitions are documented with an explicit reference to the
underlying paper in the function's \code{@details} block.

## Temperature indices

Four threshold-exceedance counters cover the core temperature
indices. Cold extremes are counted by \code{ck\_frost\_days()}
(minimum below $0^\circ$C) and \code{ck\_ice\_days()} (daytime
maximum below zero). Hot extremes are counted by
\code{ck\_summer\_days()} (maximum at or above 25) and
\code{ck\_tropical\_nights()} (minimum at or above 20).

Three degree-day accumulators report cumulative heat above or below
a reference temperature. Agricultural work uses
\code{ck\_growing\_degree\_days()} to sum degree-days above a
user-specified base. Energy-demand applications use the heating and
cooling counterparts, \code{ck\_heating\_degree\_days()} and
\code{ck\_cooling\_degree\_days()}.

\code{ck\_diurnal\_range()} reports the mean daily temperature
range. \code{ck\_growing\_season()} returns the frost-free growing
season length. \code{ck\_warm\_spell()} counts days in spells
exceeding a high-percentile threshold. Figure
\ref{fig:central-park} in the case study below shows these indices
applied to seventy-five years of real NOAA data from the New York
Central Park station.

## Precipitation and drought indices

\code{ck\_total\_precip()}, \code{ck\_dry\_days()}, and
\code{ck\_wet\_days()} summarise accumulation and spell counts.
\code{ck\_heavy\_precip()} and \code{ck\_very\_heavy\_precip()}
count exceedances of user-specified thresholds.
\code{ck\_max\_1day\_precip()} and \code{ck\_max\_5day\_precip()}
return rolling maxima. \code{ck\_precip\_intensity()} returns the
simple daily intensity index.

Figure \ref{fig:precip} shows two precipitation indices on the
Central Park station's daily record from 1950 to 2024: annual total
precipitation (blue) and the count of heavy-precipitation days
with daily total above 10 mm (red, scaled by 50 for visual
comparability). Both trend upward over the seventy-five-year
window: the annual total rises by about 45 mm per decade and the
heavy-precipitation day count by 1.15 days per decade, consistent
with the expected intensification of the hydrological cycle under
continental-US warming documented in @alexander2006global and
@donat2013hadex2.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig2_precip.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Annual precipitation indices for New York Central Park (GHCND station USW00094728), 1950 to 2024.} Blue solid: annual total precipitation in millimetres, linear trend $+45$ mm per decade. Red dashed: count of days with daily total above 10 mm, scaled by 50 for visual comparability, linear trend $+1.15$ days per decade. Dotted lines are OLS trend fits. Both indices rise over the period.}
\label{fig:precip}
\end{figure}

\code{ck\_spi()} returns the Standardised Precipitation Index at a
user-specified accumulation scale (most commonly 3, 6, or 12
months). Short-scale SPI captures short-term wet and dry spells;
long-scale SPI smooths out noise and reveals sustained anomalies.
Values below $-1$ flag moderate drought; below $-2$, extreme
drought. \code{ck\_spei()} computes the Standardised
Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index, using \code{ck\_pet()} for
potential evapotranspiration via the @hargreaves1985reference
method.

## Agroclimatic indices

\code{ck\_huglin()} returns the Huglin heliothermal index,
accumulated from April through September (Northern Hemisphere) from
daily maximum and mean temperatures weighted by a latitude
correction. \code{ck\_winkler()} returns the Winkler index (a
simpler cumulative growing-degree-day measure used in California
viticulture). \code{ck\_branas()} returns the Branas product index.
\code{ck\_first\_frost()} and \code{ck\_last\_frost()} report frost
dates each year.

Figure \ref{fig:huglin} shows the Huglin index on the synthetic
temperate site. Grey horizontal bands mark approximate viticultural
classification ranges; the site plots within the Cool to Temperate
range in most years of the sample.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_huglin.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Huglin heliothermal index on a 10-year synthetic temperate site at latitude 51.5$^\circ$N.} Shaded horizontal bands mark approximate viticultural suitability ranges: below 1500 is too cool, 1500 to 1800 is Cool (HI-3, suitable for early-ripening varieties), 1800 to 2100 is Temperate, 2100 to 2400 is Warm, above 2400 is Hot. The sample falls mostly in the Cool range.}
\label{fig:huglin}
\end{figure}

## Comfort indices

Four comfort functions cover hot and cold extremes.
\code{ck\_heat\_index()} returns the US National Weather Service
heat index (apparent temperature) from mean temperature and
relative humidity. \code{ck\_humidex()} returns the Canadian
humidex from the same inputs. \code{ck\_wind\_chill()} returns wind
chill from temperature and wind speed. \code{ck\_fire\_danger()}
returns a linearised approximation of the Canadian Fire Weather
Index (CFFWIS) combining temperature, relative humidity, wind
speed, and precipitation. The implementation is intentionally a
simplified surrogate for rapid daily computation; users requiring
the full iterative CFFWIS should pair with the specialised
\CRANpkg{cffdrs} package.

## Drought and pluvial episodes

\code{ck\_spi()} and \code{ck\_spei()} return the Standardized
Precipitation Index (McKee et al., 1993) and the Standardized
Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (Vicente-Serrano et al.,
2010). Both are unitless anomalies scaled to standard deviations: a
value of $-1$ sits one standard deviation below the long-run mean
for that calendar month, commonly interpreted as moderate drought,
and values below $-2$ as severe drought. The index is computed by
fitting a gamma distribution to rolling accumulated precipitation
totals and transforming to standard normal deviates, separately
for each calendar month to remove seasonality.

Figure \ref{fig:spi} applies \code{ck\_spi()} at a twelve-month
scale to the 1950-to-2024 daily precipitation record at New York
Central Park (NOAA GHCND USW00094728, the same station used in
the case study below). The 1960s Northeast drought is visible as
an extended run of deeply negative values between 1962 and 1966,
the most severe drought episode in the station's recorded
history. The 2001-02 drought is also clearly marked. The upper
tail is populated by well-known wet years, including 1972,
1983-84, and 2011.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_heat.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Twelve-month Standardized Precipitation Index for New York Central Park, 1950 to 2024.} Computed with \code{ck\_spi(scale = 12)} on the full GHCND USW00094728 daily precipitation record. Dashed horizontal lines at $\pm 1$ mark the moderate drought and moderate wet thresholds. The 1960s Northeast drought (1962-1966) and 2001-02 drought are the two deepest dry episodes; 2011 is the wettest year in the sample.}
\label{fig:spi}
\end{figure}

## Case study: 75 years of Central Park temperature indices

Figure \ref{fig:central-park} applies \CRANpkg{climatekit} to real
NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCND) data from
the New York Central Park station (USW00094728) from 1950 to 2024,
a seventy-five-year daily record with zero missing observations in
$T_{\min}$, $T_{\max}$, and precipitation. Three temperature
indices are computed directly from the raw daily vectors: frost
days, summer days, and growing degree days at base 10. A linear
trend fitted over the sample returns a decline of 2.6 frost days
per decade, a rise of 28 growing-degree-days per decade, and a
roughly stable summer-days count. The signs and magnitudes are
consistent with the observed warming trends for the US Northeast
documented in @alexander2006global and @donat2013hadex2. The full
computation is three function calls on three vectors.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig6_central_park.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Three temperature indices for New York Central Park (GHCND station USW00094728), 1950 to 2024.} Annual counts from raw daily $T_{\min}$, $T_{\max}$, and $T_{\mathrm{mean}}$. Blue solid: frost days ($T_{\min} < 0^\circ\mathrm{C}$), linear trend $-2.6$ days per decade. Red dashed: summer days ($T_{\max} \geq 25^\circ\mathrm{C}$), trend $+0.3$ days per decade. Green dotdash: growing degree days above base $10^\circ\mathrm{C}$, divided by 20 for visual scale, trend $+28$ GDD per decade. Dotted lines are OLS trend fits.}
\label{fig:central-park}
\end{figure}

## Replication

Table \ref{tab:families} lists the thirty indices grouped into five
families. The representative function names give the flavour of the
interface.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{\textbf{Index families in \CRANpkg{climatekit}, with count and representative function names.} All functions share the \code{ck\_} prefix and return a data frame with columns \code{period}, \code{value}, \code{index}, \code{unit}.}
\label{tab:families}
\input{tables/families.tex}
\end{table}

The canonical workflow is four lines:

```r
library(climatekit)
frost_days <- ck_frost_days(tmin, dates, period = "annual")
spi3       <- ck_spi(precip, dates, scale = 3)
huglin     <- ck_huglin(tmin, tmax, dates, lat = 51.5)
```

Each call returns a tidy data frame that can be bound directly into
a panel with other indices or plotted without reshaping.

## Limitations

Five limitations apply.

1. \CRANpkg{climatekit} computes indices from daily observations.
   Sub-daily (hourly) indices, including heat-wave indices based on
   night-time minimum temperatures and apparent-temperature
   exceedances, are not implemented.
2. Gridded-climate input is not natively supported. Users must
   reduce a gridded product to a per-cell time series before passing
   it in. For CMIP6 and similar model output,
   \CRANpkg{terra}-based preprocessing is the natural partner.
3. The SPI and SPEI implementations use the gamma distribution as
   the parametric family. Users studying very arid regions may
   prefer the Pearson III family favoured by @vicente2010multiscalar;
   this is not currently exposed.
4. Quality control is the user's responsibility. Missing-value
   handling propagates \code{NA} through the aggregation functions;
   users should screen input data for known stations-of-concern
   flags before computing indices.
5. Station homogenisation is not implemented. Detecting
   inhomogeneities (relocation, instrument change) in a daily
   record requires specialised techniques that are out of scope.

\FloatBarrier

## Appendix: index definitions

Selected formulas used by \CRANpkg{climatekit}. Daily observations
are indexed by $t$; aggregations run over a reporting window
$\mathcal{T}$ (year, month, or season).

**Frost days.** $\mathrm{FD} = \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \mathbf{1}\{T_{\min,t} < 0^\circ\mathrm{C}\}$.

**Growing degree days (base $b$).**
$\mathrm{GDD}_b = \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \max(T_{\mathrm{mean},t} - b, 0)$.

**Huglin heliothermal index.** For latitude $\phi$ and
northern-hemisphere summation over 1 April to 30 September,
$$\mathrm{HI} = K(\phi) \sum_{t = \mathrm{Apr}}^{\mathrm{Sep}}
  \frac{(T_{\mathrm{mean},t} - 10) + (T_{\max,t} - 10)}{2},$$
where $K(\phi)$ is Huglin's day-length correction ranging from 1.02
at $40^\circ$N to 1.06 at $50^\circ$N.

**Standardised Precipitation Index.** For precipitation $P_s$ summed
over an $s$-month window, fit a two-parameter gamma distribution to
the historical distribution of $P_s$ with shape $\alpha$ and scale
$\beta$, compute the non-exceedance probability
$F(P_s; \alpha, \beta)$, and transform to a standard normal:
$\mathrm{SPI}_s = \Phi^{-1}(F(P_s; \alpha, \beta))$.
Values below $-1$ indicate moderate drought; below $-2$, extreme
drought. The gamma-family default follows @stagge2015candidate.

**Heat index (US NWS, Rothfusz form).** For air temperature
$T$ in $^\circ\mathrm{F}$ and relative humidity $R$ in per cent,
$$\mathrm{HI} = c_1 + c_2 T + c_3 R + c_4 TR
  + c_5 T^2 + c_6 R^2 + c_7 T^2 R + c_8 T R^2 + c_9 T^2 R^2,$$
with the nine Rothfusz coefficients (Rothfusz 1990). The package
converts °C inputs internally.

## Conclusion

Climate-index computation is a daily activity in meteorological
services, climate research, agricultural consultancies, and
insurance underwriting, and the R ecosystem had not had a single
unified implementation. \CRANpkg{climatekit} consolidates thirty
indices across temperature, precipitation, drought, agroclimatology,
and thermal comfort behind a tidy-data-frame output format. The
package is pure R, has no data dependencies, and returns output
that composes directly into downstream analysis. Planned additions
include hourly heat-wave indices, gridded-input helpers, and
additional fire-weather variants. Contributions and bug reports are
welcome at
\url{https://github.com/charlescoverdale/climatekit}.

## Acknowledgements {-}

The CCl/WCRP/JCOMM Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and
Indices (ETCCDI) and its successor the Expert Team on
Sector-specific Climate Indices (ET-SCI) developed and documented
the index definitions on which this package is built. The National
Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration publishes the Global
Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCND) dataset that is the
natural input source for these indices.
